Hook: Wednesday the sixteenth of September 1992, in four acts. In the morning the Bank of England raises its interest rate from ten percent to twelve. Nothing happens; the pound keeps falling. In the afternoon it announces fifteen percent, to take effect the next day. Still nothing. All day it buys pounds with its foreign currency reserves, by the billion. Papers released by the Treasury in 2005 put the eventual cost at about three point three billion pounds. In the evening the Chancellor of the Exchequer, Norman Lamont, announces that sterling's membership of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism is suspended. The rise to fifteen percent never takes effect.

Here is the contradiction. In October 1990 Britain had joined the Exchange Rate Mechanism at two point nine five German marks to the pound, promising to keep within six percent either side. By the summer of 1992 the pound was near the bottom of its band. Germany, paying for unification, kept its interest rates high; Britain, in recession, needed lower ones, and could not cut them without breaking the band. When the attack came, the reserves went first. Then the peg. Between August and October the pound fell 13 percent against the mark, and within five months British interest rates were down from 10 percent to 6. The speculators, George Soros most famously, did not cause the contradiction. They found it.

This part's question: what sets the price of one money in terms of another, and what can a country not have at once? What pins an exchange rate down: the prices of goods, interest rates, or nothing at all? Why can a country not fix its currency, let capital move freely and set its own interest rate, all three? And why do currencies crash, and who runs the world's money?
Economics, Built. Part thirty-four: the open economy.

Act seven opens the economy to the world, and here is this part's plan. The balance of payments, and a game: you are the governor of a central bank under attack. What should pin exchange rates down, prices and interest rates, and how badly both fail in the data, down to the uncomfortable fact that no model beats a coin-toss forecast. The model every policymaker carries, Mundell and Fleming's, with its trilemma, and Dornbusch's overshooting. Currency crises in three generations, the IMF, and the euro. Global imbalances, the dollar's peculiar role, and two dials.
BOP: Chapter one. The balance of payments.

Start with accounting, because in international economics it settles more arguments than theory does. Every purchase from abroad has to be paid for, so a country's dealings with the world must balance. The current account, exports minus imports plus net income from abroad, and the financial account, what a country sells of its assets to foreigners, add up to zero. A country that imports more than it exports is selling assets, or borrowing, to pay. The national accounts of Part three give the same thing another way. Output is spent on consumption, investment, government purchases and net exports, so the current account is national saving minus investment. A deficit is not a loss or a scorecard. It is a country investing more than it saves, and borrowing the difference.

America is the largest example. It has run a current account deficit every year of this century, widest at 6.2 percent of GDP in 2006, and 3.0 percent now. The financial account is the other side: Americans have sold assets to foreigners and borrowed from them every year, so the country's net position against the world went from minus 12 percent of GDP in 2006 to minus 69 percent now. Whether that is a problem depends on what the borrowing paid for, what the debts cost, and what currency they are in. For the United States, as chapter eleven shows, the answers are unusual.
PPP: If goods can be shipped, the same good should cost the same everywhere once prices are converted at the exchange rate: the law of one price. Apply it to everything and you get purchasing power parity: exchange rates should move to equalize price levels. Since 1986 The Economist has tested this with one good that is the same everywhere, the Big Mac. In America it costs 6.22 dollars. In Switzerland, converted at the market rate, 9.04: on this measure the franc is 45 percent overvalued. In India, 2.45, which would make the rupee 61 percent undervalued. The gaps are enormous and they last. A burger is not a ship's cargo.

Part of the pattern is systematic. Plot each currency's Big Mac valuation against the country's income per head. Richer countries tend to have dearer burgers. Bela Balassa and Paul Samuelson explained why in 1964. Productivity in traded goods is much higher in rich countries, and that sets their wages. Services, like flipping burgers, are not much more productive there, but they must pay the same wages, so services cost more. The tilt is real but loose: a slope of 0.08 and a correlation of 0.29 across 51 countries in the latest survey. Much of the spread is something else.

Does parity hold in the long run? Here is Britain's real exchange rate against the dollar since 1870: the pound's purchasing power in America relative to at home. It wanders far from its average, for years, and comes back. Fitting how fast deviations shrink across eighteen countries, half of a deviation is gone after 5.2 years over the whole period, and after 2.6 years since the floating era began in 1973. Kenneth Rogoff's survey of 1996 put the consensus at three to five years, and called it a puzzle. Deviations that large and that persistent cannot be explained by prices that are sticky for a year or so; but exchange rates swing far too much from month to month to be explained by real shocks. Exchange rates return toward parity, slowly.
UIP: Chapter four. Interest parity and the carry trade.

Exchange rates are asset prices, so the next idea comes from finance. An investor with dollars for a year can hold dollars and earn the dollar interest rate, or change them into pounds, earn the British rate, and change back at whatever the exchange rate is next year. If the rate to change back is fixed today, with a forward contract, the two must pay the same, or there is free money; this covered parity holds closely, apart from strains in and since 2008. If it is not fixed, and investors care only about the expected return, the same logic gives uncovered parity: a currency paying a higher interest rate should be expected to fall, by just the gap, so that no one gains by chasing high rates.

Eugene Fama tested it in 1984. Regress the change in a currency's value over the next three months on the interest gap at the start. Uncovered parity says the slope is one. Here are the slopes for seven currencies against the dollar since 1979, recomputed from the data. 6 of the 7 are below zero. High-interest currencies did not fall by the gap; on average they tended to rise. The bands are wide, because exchange rates are so noisy, but the pattern has been found in nearly every sample since: the forward premium puzzle.

If high-rate currencies do not fall, there is money in borrowing where rates are low and lending where they are high: the carry trade. Each month, hold the two highest-yielding of these eight currencies, the dollar among them, and borrow the two lowest. Since 1985 this has earned 4.2 percent a year above the cost of funds, with a Sharpe ratio of 0.57, about that of the stock market. But not smoothly. Its worst month was 2008's autumn, minus 11 percent, when the yen, the cheapest currency to borrow, soared and the Australian and New Zealand dollars, the favourite targets, fell, as everyone closed the same trade at once. Traders say carry goes up by the stairs and down by the lift. Perhaps the return is simply pay for bearing crash risk, and parity holds once that is priced; that is one of the leading explanations of the puzzle.
Meese: If parity conditions explain so little, can anything forecast exchange rates? In 1983 Richard Meese and Kenneth Rogoff ran a horse race. They took the leading models of the day, gave them the actual values of everything the models said should matter, and asked them to forecast exchange rates one to twelve months ahead. None beat the simplest forecast of all: no change, the random walk. Here is the race rerun. Each month since 1990, for the pound, the yen, the Canadian dollar and the Swiss franc, three forecasts are made using only data available then: no change; the change interest parity predicts; and a statistical model fitted to the last ten years of monthly moves. The bars are each forecast's error relative to the random walk's. At one month, three months and a year, they are all within a fraction of a percent of one. The random walk's own errors are 2.5 percent at a month and 8.4 at a year. Forty years after Meese and Rogoff, their result still mostly stands: at short horizons, exchange rates behave like a random walk.
Dornbusch: Exchange rates swing far more than the fundamentals behind them. Rudiger Dornbusch showed in 1976 that this needs no irrationality. Goods prices move slowly; asset prices move at once. In the money market, more money relative to prices must be held at a lower interest rate. And by interest parity, a lower interest rate at home must be matched by an expected rise in the currency's value. Now the central bank raises the money supply for good. In the long run prices and the exchange rate rise in proportion. But today prices cannot move, so the interest rate falls, and for investors to hold the currency at that lower rate it must be expected to appreciate from here on. The only way both can be true is for the currency to fall today by more than it will in the end. On the Island's numbers, the currency jumps 1.5 times as far as its final resting place.

Here is the path. The money supply rises ten percent at time zero. The currency's price jumps 15 percent at once, while prices start to rise only slowly. As prices catch up, the interest rate recovers and the currency appreciates back toward its new level, ten percent above the old. Overshooting, in the data, is weaker and slower than in the model; Part thirty-one's identification problem makes it hard to measure, and the forward premium puzzle of chapter four suggests the expected appreciation is not there. But the mechanism explains why exchange rates move so much on news about policy.
Crises: Chapter eight. Currency crises, three generations.

The first generation of models, Paul Krugman's of 1979, explains crises in Latin America. A government pegs its currency but prints money to pay for a deficit; the new money is swapped for foreign currency at the central bank, and reserves drain, steadily. At every moment there is a shadow exchange rate: where the currency would float if reserves were gone. It rises as money is printed. Speculators do not wait for reserves to run out. The moment the shadow rate reaches the peg, holding the currency becomes a losing bet, and they buy the remaining reserves in a single attack: here in year 15, not year 20, when the drain would have finished on its own. The crisis looks sudden; its cause was years old. And the peg falls without any jump in the exchange rate, because the attack comes exactly when there is none to profit from.

Each generation of models was written after the crises it explains. The first: bad fundamentals, a predictable attack. The second, after 1992: governments that could defend a peg but might choose not to, so that attacks can succeed because they are expected. In September 1992 Sweden's central bank raised its overnight rate to five hundred percent for a few days to defend the krona; by November it had let it float too. The third, after Asia in 1997: balance sheets. Firms and banks with debts in dollars are bankrupted by the devaluation itself, so currency crises and banking crises arrive together, the twin crises Graciela Kaminsky and Carmen Reinhart documented. Black Wednesday belongs to the second generation. Britain's reserves and credit were not exhausted. Holding the peg would have meant still higher interest rates in a recession, and the markets judged, correctly, that the government would not pay that price.
Imbalances: Chapter one's identity says a deficit is investment above saving. Across the world, the deficits and surpluses must match. In the 2000s they grew large: America's deficit reached 5.8 percent of GDP in 2006; China's surplus 10 percent in 2007; and later Germany's 8 percent, in 2015. Was America spending too much, or the rest of the world saving too much? In March 2005 Ben Bernanke, then a Fed governor, argued the second: a global saving glut, as Asian economies built reserves after 1997 and oil exporters saved their windfalls, pushed money into American assets and held down interest rates, which fed the housing boom of Part thirty-three.

America's position has a peculiar feature. In the 1960s the French finance minister, Valery Giscard d'Estaing, called it an exorbitant privilege. The United States borrows in its own currency, cheaply, by selling the safe assets the rest of the world wants to hold. Pierre-Olivier Gourinchas and Helene Rey showed that it earns more on what it owns abroad, shares and firms, than it pays on what it owes, mostly safe bonds: it is the world's banker, borrowing short and safe and lending long and risky. So a net position of minus 69 percent of GDP costs less than it looks, and in global crises, when its risky assets fall and its safe debts rise in value, America pays out, like an insurer. Ricardo Caballero, Emmanuel Farhi and Gourinchas argue that the world is short of safe assets, and that this shortage explains low interest rates and the dollar's strength in every panic, including one that started in America.
Dollar: Much of the world's trade is priced in dollars, even trade that never touches America. Gita Gopinath and coauthors call it the dominant currency paradigm, and it changes how exchange rates work. When the dollar rises ten percent, what happens to the dollar prices of what America imports? Estimated month by month, the answer here is: almost nothing at once, 0.04 of the change, and 0.44 after a year. Because the prices were set in dollars, the dollar's moves barely reach American buyers. Gopinath, Oleg Itskhoki and Roberto Rigobon found pass-through of a quarter for goods priced in dollars and nearly all of it for goods priced in other currencies. The corollary is uncomfortable for the rest of the world: when a country's currency falls against the dollar, its imports become dearer at once, but its exports, priced in dollars, do not get cheaper.

The dollar's reach goes beyond trade. Here is a measure of fear on Wall Street, the VIX. When it rises, capital flows out of emerging markets everywhere at once, credit tightens and asset prices fall together: one global financial cycle. Helene Rey showed in 2013 that this cycle moves with the Federal Reserve's policy. Her conclusion was that the trilemma is really a dilemma: a floating exchange rate does not protect a country from the cycle if capital moves freely, so the real choice is between open capital markets and control of your own financial conditions, with the macroprudential tools of Part thirty-three as the middle way.

And the largest currency that does not float. China held the yuan at 8.28 to the dollar until July 2005, then let it rise slowly, to 6.85 by 2008, and held it there through the financial crisis. In August 2015 a small devaluation, under two percent, set off a scare in markets everywhere, and capital flowed out until controls were tightened. China sits at the trilemma's third corner: a managed exchange rate and its own monetary policy, bought with limits on capital. Whether the yuan can rival the dollar depends on giving up those limits, which would mean giving up one of the other two.
